title: Activating ZIA changes from Terraform: methods, session end and concurrent applies

checks.do: Whether the run outlived the API session timeout when changes went live before the apply finished.
Whether `zia_activation_status` lists every resource or module it must follow in `depends_on`.
Whether more than one apply targets the tenant at once, before blaming rate limits for slow writes.

tenant-wide-call.statement: The provider documentation says a single ZIA activation call publishes every pending change in the tenant, regardless of how many resources Terraform created, updated or deleted.

quotes: Activation is a tenant-wide operation, not a per-resource one.
regardless of how many resources Terraform created, updated, or deleted

three-methods.statement: The provider documents three activation methods in order of preference: the out-of-band `ziaActivator` CLI, the `zia_activation_status` resource, and the `ZIA_ACTIVATION` environment variable.

quotes: The provider supports three activation methods, described below in order of preference.
### Method 1 — Out-of-band activation with the `ziaActivator` CLI (recommended)
### Method 3 — The `ZIA_ACTIVATION` environment variable (discouraged)

activator-one-call.statement: The `ziaActivator` CLI is recommended for CI/CD and large configurations: it issues exactly one activation call for the whole run, run after Terraform finishes, and adds no activation traffic to the apply.

quotes: This is the recommended method for CI/CD pipelines and for large configurations.
It issues exactly one activation call for the entire run

status-resource-needs-depends-on.statement: `zia_activation_status` cannot infer its dependencies: every resource whose changes must be activated has to be listed in `depends_on`, and a resource left out may be applied after activation and stay pending.

quotes: `depends_on` cannot be inferred
every resource whose changes must be activated has to be listed explicitly
therefore left pending

env-method-discouraged.statement: `ZIA_ACTIVATION=true` is discouraged and may be removed in a future major release: it triggers an activation call for every resource created, updated or deleted.

quotes: This method is discouraged and may be removed in a future major release.
It triggers an activation call for **every** resource created, updated, or deleted

activation-endpoint-budget.statement: The provider documentation gives the activation endpoint a budget of 10 POST requests per minute and 40 per hour, which a configuration of any meaningful size exhausts when every resource activates in flight.

quotes: at **10 POST requests per minute and 40 per hour**

session-end-autoactivation.statement: The ZIA platform activates pending changes on its own when a session ends, either because an API session reached the `api_session_timeout` or because an admin logged out; this applies to all API changes, including Terraform's.

quotes: The ZIA platform has its own auto-activation behavior, independent of the Terraform provider.
or because an admin logged out

session-timeout-range.statement: The API session timeout accepts 5 to 20 minutes and defaults to 5.

quotes: It accepts **5 to 20 minutes and defaults to 5**.

mid-run-activation.statement: A Terraform run longer than the API session timeout crosses a session boundary and has its pending changes activated part-way through, before the apply has written the rest; the provider then opens a new session and continues without failing.

quotes: will cross that boundary and have its pending changes activated part-way through
The provider then establishes a new session and continues, so the run does not fail

autoactivation-cannot-be-disabled.statement: Activation on session end is native to the platform and cannot be disabled or overridden by the provider; a higher timeout only reduces how often a long run crosses a boundary.

quotes: activation on session end is native to the platform and cannot be disabled or overridden by the provider

raise-timeout-to-20.statement: The guidance for large configurations is to raise the API session timeout to its 20 minute maximum, in the admin portal or with `api_session_timeout` on `zia_advanced_settings`, and to split very large work across smaller states.

quotes: Raise the timeout to its maximum of 20 minutes before running large configurations.
Set the `api_session_timeout` attribute on the `zia_advanced_settings` resource
split the work across smaller states

activator-does-not-suppress.statement: Running `ziaActivator` once at the end of a pipeline therefore does not suppress session-end autoactivation during the apply.
activator-does-not-suppress.conditions: Inferred from the activator being a separate call after the apply and the platform behavior being outside the provider's control.

one-apply-per-tenant.statement: A tenant has a single configuration-change lock and a single activation queue, so plans can run in parallel (reads do not take the lock) but only one write-bearing apply should run against a tenant at a time, with CI concurrency keyed on the tenant.

quotes: **Apply one configuration at a time** against a given tenant.
Read operations do not take the write lock, so planning several configurations concurrently is safe.
using a CI concurrency control keyed on the **tenant**

lock-errors-retried.statement: Requests that cannot take the write lock are rejected with `EDIT_LOCK_NOT_AVAILABLE`, `Resource Access Blocked` or `Failed during enter Org barrier`; the provider retries them automatically, so contention usually appears as a slower run rather than an error.

quotes: `EDIT_LOCK_NOT_AVAILABLE`, `Resource Access Blocked`, or `Failed during enter Org barrier`
contention typically appears as a progressively slower run rather than an immediate failure

do-not-lower-parallelism.statement: Lowering Terraform's `-parallelism` does not reduce the number of competing runs, and the longer run increases the chance of crossing an API session boundary.

quotes: Do not lower Terraform's `-parallelism` in response to lock contention.

activation-queues.statement: A queued activation waits until every editing administrator or API session has activated and cannot be cancelled, so activating at the end of each configuration does not publish that configuration independently.

quotes: a queued activation cannot be cancelled
publication timing is set by whichever run finishes last

queue-publishes-partial-runs.statement: When the queue clears, all pending tenant changes are published, including those from a run still in progress or one that failed part-way, so a partially created rule set can take effect with incomplete ordering.

quotes: a partially created rule set can take effect with incomplete ordering

separate-tenant-boundary.statement: A separate tenant is the only boundary that gives truly concurrent execution, since each tenant has its own write lock and activation queue.

quotes: a separate tenant is the only boundary that provides it
